query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent, slow-growing protective oxide layer forms and persists above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than cracking or spalling? Earlier work investigated CrFeCoNiX and CrMoTiAlY (Y = Ta, Nb, or W) alloy systems and reported that some compositions developed unstable surface oxides prone to cracking and spallation, while the underlying physical causes remain unresolved. Given the requirement for an environmentally stable, chemically inert barrier and prolonged structural integrity, specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted observations, the relevant composition, material-state, exposure, and service boundaries, the prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, the identity of the X element governs the formation and stability of the protective oxide layer at >900 °C: specifically, when X = Al, preferential oxidation leads to the in situ formation of a coherent, slow-growing alumina-rich oxide layer that adheres well to the substrate, whereas when X = Si or Mn, the resulting oxides have poorer lattice matching and higher thermal expansion mismatch with the metallic matrix, causing stresses that lead to cracking and spallation.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (either single-phase or multiphase solid-solution states) with X being Al, Si, or Mn, fabricated under controlled conditions to achieve comparable microstructures.
generation.intervention: Exposure to an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C for a sufficient period to promote scale formation.
generation.conditions: Temperature >900 °C, controlled oxygen partial pressure (or corrosive gas environment), exposure duration reflective of high-temperature service conditions, and similar thermal cycling protocols for all alloy variants.
generation.structural_mediator: The composition and microstructure of the oxide scale – particularly its lattice coherence and adhesion to the substrate – mediate whether the oxide remains stable or undergoes cracking/spallation.
generation.mechanism: In alloys with X = Al, the high affinity of Al for oxygen results in the formation of a dense, slow-growing alumina-rich oxide that is coherent with the underlying lattice, minimizing stress accumulation. In contrast, in alloys with X = Si or Mn, the oxides formed exhibit greater lattice mismatch and higher thermal expansion differences with the substrate, leading to stress accumulation, crack inception, and eventual spallation of the scale.
generation.predicted_outcome: Upon high-temperature exposure, CrFeCoNiAl alloys will develop a stable, adherent, and slow-growing oxide scale, while CrFeCoNiSi and CrFeCoNiMn alloys will show evidence of oxide cracking, spallation, or delamination.
generation.baseline: The baseline is the behavior of CrFeCoNiX alloys that do not form a protective oxide layer under identical high-temperature oxidative conditions, typically characterized by rapid oxide growth, poor adherence, and spallation.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to high-entropy alloys within the CrFeCoNiX family (X = Al, Si, or Mn) subjected to temperatures above 900 °C in oxidizing or corrosive environments, with the microstructural state controlled by appropriate synthesis (e.g., powder metallurgy or spark plasma sintering) to yield similar phase distributions.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty about the precise kinetics of oxide scale growth and the quantitative thresholds of composition and microstructural features required for optimal oxide adherence, as well as potential influences from minor secondary phases in multiphase alloys.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate three sets of CrFeCoNiX alloys where X is Al, Si, and Mn, respectively, ensuring similar initial microstructures and phase compositions. Expose samples from each set to an oxidizing atmosphere at temperatures >900 °C under identical conditions (e.g., same duration, oxygen partial pressure, and thermal cycling protocols). After exposure, characterize the surface and cross-sectional oxide layers using X-ray diffraction, SEM (with EDS), and adhesion tests.
measurements: Oxide layer thickness and growth rate
Crystal structure and phase composition of the oxide
Microstructural coherence and adhesion between the oxide scale and the substrate
Extent and frequency of spallation or cracking (via microscopy and surface profilometry)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If CrFeCoNiAl samples do not exhibit a significantly more coherent, adherent, and slow-growing oxide layer compared to the CrFeCoNiSi and CrFeCoNiMn samples (i.e., if all three compositions display similar oxide instability or if Si/Mn alloys unexpectedly show stable scales), then the hypothesis is falsified.
